title: Importance of recording the Kansas City years
summary: Leeman and Jo Jones never talk about Kansas City because no one would understand; Hinton stresses the importance of the record and Leeman calls it a hot bed of jazz.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: But there were a few people there, few who witnessed this like you did -- this is why the Smithsonian would like to have it in your own voice.

Well, Jo Jones -- if we were in a club or something, Jo just looks at me and if there are any other people around, he says, "Kansas City?" and he shakes his head, and I shake my head -- no sense in talking about it because nobody would know what we were talking about.

But it's important that somebody should know. Now we have Jo on record and we have you on record, and these things coincide, which is just beautiful. All your years are exactly the same years that Jo talks about, and about the Kansas City -- and of course, I was there at that same period, and I have been through that, too.
No, I was with Cab Calloway. And all of these things coincide, and it's so very important that, for posterity that these things be recorded.

Then there are other people who I heard that I couldn't digest, because I didn't remember until later years, like Johnson was there -- oh, it's just impossible, you have to go through the archives of jazz to find out who was living there and playing there then.

(UNINTELLIGIBLE) and they came over to Chicago; I can tell you the years that they came to Chicago from Kansas City, because the whole migration was south and the middle west, and Chicago, which was the hot bed of jazz, even before New York.
Some people think that jazz started in New Orleans. But we won't get into that controversial thing.

But the middle west, Kansas City -- it was just alive, it was like a hot bed -- all these great musicians that came out of there in that era, and God was wonderful to me that He took me there, and I believe that He said, 'This is it' and He just wanted me to be there, and it's like anything else. I was there at the right time, at the right place at the right time.

Well, you were there, and besides that in all the annals of history, you are without a doubt the only white drummer that came up, because you knew all of these people that you have been involved with because of the association -- how you got from this town in the New England states to Kansas City is a miracle, through Dan Murphy in Boston, which is as different as night and day. And here you are, in all of the annals of drumming, all the great drummers of the jazz era -- you, Cliff Leeman, have bridged the biggest gap, and in a society in which jazz is

considered a black art, you have been around longer and before most of them have been involved with most black artists and most black performers, and you have been involved with Basie, in Kansas City with Dave Tough, Jo Jones, Gene Austin Jim Krupa, with Baby Dodds, Buddy Rich and Cubie? -- Sid Catlett these are -- and Big . So here you are -- your name ranks high among all the other drummers that I just named, and I'm certain that there are more that you can tell me about, because I can't tell you about your profession -- but your name ranks high in there and here is a record as proof of where you came in, before Jo Jones in Kansas City.
